summary: CoAP is a RESTful protocol for constrained nodes, and basic messages work well for small payloads but sometimes larger ones are needed, such as firmware updates. This proposed standard defines block-wise transfers, which let a large resource be sent as a series of smaller blocks without needing the network to fragment packets.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7959 adds Block1 and Block2 options so CoAP can transfer a large representation as smaller pieces. Each block uses a separate request and response, which avoids relying on IP fragmentation and allows a missing block to be retried.

questions: how does coap send large payloads
what is the coap block2 option
what block sizes does coap support
subtitle: Move large CoAP representations in small, separately acknowledged pieces.

tldr.problem: A CoAP message may be too large for a constrained network, and relying on lower-layer fragmentation puts extra state and recovery work below the application.
tldr.mechanism: Block1 and Block2 options identify the number, size, and finality of request or response blocks; each block is carried in its own CoAP exchange.
tldr.outcome: Endpoints can transfer large representations and retransmit individual blocks. Atomic updates may require server state, while stateless updates can expose partial content.

today: RFC 7959 is a Proposed Standard and updates RFC 7252. It is later updated by RFC 8323.

sections.title: Why CoAP Uses Blocks
sections.content:
CoAP runs over datagram transports and is designed for constrained devices and networks. Large representations can exceed the size that is practical to send in one message, while IP or adaptation-layer fragmentation puts reassembly state in lower layers.

RFC 7959 moves this work into CoAP. It divides the representation into blocks sent as a sequence of ordinary CoAP request-response exchanges.
sections.plainLanguage: A large CoAP response may not fit in one packet that a constrained network can carry reliably. Block-wise transfer sends it in smaller pieces at the application layer.

sections.title: Block1, Block2, and Their Fields
sections.content:
Block1 describes the request body, and Block2 describes the response body. Each option encodes a block number (NUM), a More bit (M), and a size exponent (SZX). The number starts at zero, and the M bit indicates whether more blocks follow.

SZX values from 0 to 6 represent block sizes from 16 to 1024 bytes. The sender can request a size, but the other endpoint may choose a smaller one; later requests use the size actually returned.
sections.plainLanguage: Each block option identifies which piece is being sent, whether another piece follows, and the requested block size. The receiver can ask for smaller blocks than the sender first proposed.

sections.title: Getting a Large Response
sections.content:
A server can return the first block of a response with Block2 and set M when more data is available. The client then sends more requests, naming the next block number, until the final response has M unset.

For a resource that may change during transfer, the server should include an ETag on each block. The client compares the ETags so it does not combine blocks from different versions of the representation.
sections.plainLanguage: The client requests response blocks in order and stops when the server marks the last one. Matching ETags help confirm that all pieces came from one version of the resource.

sections.title: Sending a Large Request
sections.content:
A client uses Block1 to send a large request body, such as a PUT or POST. A server that plans to apply the request atomically can answer intermediate blocks with 2.31 Continue and apply the change when the final block arrives.

A server may instead process blocks without keeping the whole request. This reduces state but can leave a resource partly changed if the transfer stops. A missing or expired block can produce 4.08 Request Entity Incomplete.
sections.plainLanguage: Block1 divides a large request into pieces. The server can wait until all pieces arrive before applying the change, or update as it goes and accept the risk of a partial result.

sections.title: Security and Resource Limits
sections.content:
Servers must apply the same security checks to every block of a protected resource. A high block number or misleading size indication can also cause a weak implementation to allocate too much memory.

Keeping state for partial requests or snapshots can expose a server to resource-exhaustion attacks. The RFC recommends minimizing state for untrusted clients and allowing partial state to time out.
sections.plainLanguage: Every piece must receive the same protection as the whole resource. Servers should limit memory and temporary state that block requests can cause them to keep.
